newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan calls Zaire human drama "slow extermination".
newsitem.headline: Annan calls Zaire human drama "slow extermination".

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Friday called the refugee crisis in eastern Zaire "slow extermination," his spokesman said.

Spokesman Fred Eckhard said there was an "increasing suspicion" that "these people are being attacked in an organised way" and that "those responsible for this treatment must be held responsible." He said the existing Rwanda war crimes tribunal could be used against the perpetrators.
"The secretary-general feels that many innocent people here are victims of a policy of slow extermination," he said.
"As long as (access) is being intentionally impeded you have to say people are intentionally allowed to die," he said.
His criticism was echoed in Geneva where a World Food Agency official accused Zaire rebels of aiming for a "final solution" in the deaths of 80,000 unwanted Rwandan Hutus.

Annan for the past few days has been speaking to about 20 governments in the region and elsewhere in an attempt to put pressure on rebel leader Laurent Kabila and his followers to get access to the refugees.
Apart from Rwanda and Uganda, which back the rebels, diplomats say the governments of the United States and Britain have varying degrees of influence on Kabila.
Most of the refugees fled in 1994 in fear of reprisals for the Hutu-led genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates. They are widely regarded as killers in their homeland.

In Geneva, Christiane Berthiaume of the World Food Programme said that 80,000 people "are condemned to a slow and cruel death. The expression 'final solution' is not exaggerated," she said, alluding to Nazi Germany's notorious policy to exterminate the Jews.
"They (the rebels) want these people to die. There's food over there but these people are starving. If the refugees go into the jungle, they will die. We are powerless."
An aerial search by the United Nations confirmed on Friday that the refugees had fled from camps in eastern Zaire sealed off from relief efforts by Laurent Kabila's rebel troops.
Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, wrote to Kabila urging an immediate search for the missing refugees. Ogata is "appalled and angry," said her spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole.
"We had up to 100,000 people identified in that area, and now we can find a trace of only a couple of thousand," she said.

Kabila's rebels, who have captured half of Zaire and appear poised to end the 31-year rule of Zaire's cancer-stricken President Mobutu Sese Seko, are accused of slaughtering Rwandan refugees in a camp south of the eastern city of Kisangani.

Diplomats said President Bill Clinton's special envoy for Africa's Great Lakes region, Richard Bogosian, had been expected to contact Kabila this week to seek support for UNHCR's stalled repatriation programme.
Aid officials say privately that the rebels delayed the plan under pressure from Rwanda's Tutsi rulers, already swamped by the return of more than half a million Hutu returnees late last year.
Many among the refugees are sick and malnourished. They were dying at a rate of 60 a day before they fled their camps.

The World Health Organisation on Friday reported 67 deaths out of 550 cholera cases as of April 19 in Kasese camp which 55,000 refugees fled. In nearby Biaro camp, empty of its 30,000 refugees, it reported two deaths out of three cholera cases.
